title: Resilience Research funding exists largely to write the legal-resilience framework the Atlas has not yet defined
content:
A.2.10.1.3 requires every Resilience Research project to serve at least one objective, and its first listed option is to "[b]ootstrap necessary infrastructure to develop one of the high-order legal resilience objectives": Legal Defense, Legal Risk Management, Privacy and Operational Security, Advocacy and Public Policy, Legal and Regulatory Risk Monitoring, Public Procurement Framework, Atlas Amendment and Audit, and Technical and Legal Standards.

Read against A.2.9, most of those objectives are currently headings over empty rooms. Privacy and Operational Security (A.2.9.1.3), Advocacy and Public Policy (A.2.9.1.4), Legal and Regulatory Risk Monitoring (A.2.9.1.5), the Public Procurement Framework (A.2.9.1.6), and the Audit Procedure for Atlas Amendments (A.2.9.1.7) are each phrased as "[t]his document defines" or "must define" a framework whose content is not present. So is A.2.9.1.1.4, the Standard Operational Protocols for reacting to legal action.

The pattern is worth naming: the Atlas fixes the *taxonomy* of legal resilience first, then funds external contributors through a grant programme to fill in the contents. A.2.10.1.4's application requirements (costs and benefits, team composition, milestones with KPIs, risk-mitigation justification) are a grant-evaluation apparatus, and A.2.10.1.5 assigns review to the Core Facilitator with published reviews for high-quality proposals.

The consequence is that the taxonomy is doing real work as a scope fence — a proposal that does not map to one of the eight objectives is out of scope regardless of merit — while the framework's substance depends on whoever applies. Progress on legal resilience is therefore supply-driven, gated by budget availability (A.2.10.1.5.1) rather than by priority.
description: Projects must serve one of eight named objectives, and 'bootstrap necessary infrastructure' is listed first
